newsitem.title: USA: Mercury Finance now estimates big 1996 loss, rather than profit.
newsitem.headline: Mercury Finance now estimates big 1996 loss, rather than profit.

text.p: Mercury Finance Co. said Wednesday that it now estimates that it lost between $48 million and $55 million last year -- rather than the $57 million profit it estimated in January -- and added that it may have to go out of business.

Mercury, which said a continuing audit of its books could raise doubts about its ability to stay in business, said the loss estimate, equal to between 28 cents and 32 cents a share, superseded its Jan. 29 estimate of a profit of $56.7 million, or 33 cents a share, for 1996.

The company, which primarily makes auto loans to relatively high-risk borrowers, also said its latest estimate was preliminary and subject to further revision as its independent auditors, Arthur Andersen LLP, continue to review its financial results.

"The company expects that the auditor's formal opinion will raise doubts about the company's ability to continue as a going concern, primarily because the company continues to be in default of its debt agreements," Mercury said in a statement.

The company said the change in estimated earnings was due primarily to additional loss provisions of $125 million and the establishment of a $25 million reserve for the loss on the pending sale of Lyndon Insurance Co.
"Management believes that the method it used to compute the loss reserves is as conservative as any used in the industry," it said.
It also said shareholder's equity as of Dec. 31 was now estimated to be between $138 million and $145 million, down from the $263 million estimated in January.
Mercury added that Arthur Andersen continued to audit its books and expected to have its opinion on 1996 results available by the end of May.
The company had said in late January that it would have to lower its reported earnings for the last four years by about $90 million due to accounting discrepancies.

Since that time, Mercury has defaulted on millions of dollars in debt, been served with a search warrant by FBI agents seeking financial records and has been named a defendant in several shareholder lawsuits.
The company lost more than $2 billion in market capitalisation when Mercury's stock plunged following the disclosure that earnings would have to be restated.

William Brandt, Mercury's president and chief executive, said that a substantial portion of the additional loss provision related to retail instalment contracts and loans originated in 1995 and prior years and that the 1996 loss provision is not indicative of future expected loss rates.
Brandt said that steps have been taken to improve the quality of newly acquired loans and retail instalment contracts, as well as to increase efforts to collect outstanding balances.

Mercury said it has a $50 million credit facility with BankAmerica Business Credit, of which $40 million is available to borrow. This facility, combined with daily cash flows, continues to provide more than sufficient working capital to operate the business and pay interest on its debt obligations, it said.
The company said also said it continues to work with its lenders concerning the amounts owed to provide for a long-term solution to its capital requirements.
Mercury's stock lost an additional 50 cents Wednesday, falling to $1.50 on the New York Stock Exchange.
